name: Nasal tanning spray
lead: Nasal tanning sprays are unlicensed products sold online that contain melanotan-type peptides, marketed as a needle-free way to darken the skin without sun exposure. The active ingredients are synthetic analogues of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), such as melanotan II, which stimulates melanin production through melanocortin receptors in skin pigment cells [1].

People use them to get a deeper tan with less time in the sun or a tanning bed, and sellers pitch the spray as an alternative to the injections more commonly associated with melanotan. In forums, users have asked whether the nasal form works at all, and one T Nation member relayed claims that a peptide's large molecular weight would make a spray ineffective [2]. Published human research on nasal delivery for tanning was not found.

Melanotan II was never marketed as a licensed drug. Health agencies including Norway's and Denmark's medicines agencies, the UK MHRA, the Irish Medicines Board and the US FDA have warned against unlicensed melanotan products, citing safety risks and potential impurities [1].
infobox: Melanotan II acts on MC1, MC3, MC4 and MC5 receptors [1]
Not approved as a medicine; regulators warn against use [1]

paras: Melanotan peptides were synthesised at the University of Arizona in the 1980s as potential sunless tanning agents [1]. Development of melanotan II was dropped by Palatin in 2000, and unlicensed versions later circulated online, in gyms and in beauty salons [1]. A related approved drug, afamelanotide (from melanotan I), was approved by the FDA in 2019 for a rare genetic form of sun sensitivity [1].
Sellers market nasal sprays as a needle-free alternative to injection. The contents of such products are not regulated and their purity and dose are not verified by any authority [1].

Melanotan II is a non-selective melanocortin receptor agonist; activating MC1 produces melanogenesis, while effects such as sexual arousal are thought to involve MC4. Palatin Technologies, which held the licence, stopped developing it in 2000 to pursue bremelanotide, and a 2008 settlement returned rights to Competitive Technologies [1].

No studies found on nasal tanning sprays. Research on melanotan II in general has examined its effects on pigmentation, sexual arousal and melanoma risk; a 2013 systematic review found no conclusive evidence that it causes melanoma, and a 2021 review concluded the higher melanoma incidence reported in users could probably be explained by more UV exposure [1].

Reported effects of melanotan II include facial flushing, nausea, vomiting, stretching, yawning, loss of appetite, spontaneous erections in men, and darkening of moles and freckles [1]. Regulators cite case reports of significant safety problems and the risk of impurities in unlicensed products [1].

Warnings began in 2007 with the Norwegian Medicines Agency (repeated 2009), followed by the Danish Medicines Agency in 2008, the MHRA in 2008, an FDA warning letter to US Lab Research Inc. on 29 January 2009, and an Irish Medicines Board notice on 27 February 2009 [1]. A 2009 BMJ paper linked changes in moles to use of an unlicensed tan jab [1].

timeline.event: University of Arizona researchers synthesise melanotan I and II as sunless tanning agents. [1]
Palatin Technologies stops developing melanotan II [1].

lore.intro: Nasal melanotan is discussed on T Nation mainly as a question of whether a spray is a workable alternative to injection [2][3].

claims.claim: Nasal sprays work as well as injected melanotan
claims.believers: Sellers and some posters present the spray as a needle-free route that gives the same tan [3].
claims.experts: No published study has tested nasal delivery of melanotan II for tanning; regulators warn that unlicensed products can contain impurities [1].

claims.claim: A melanotan-aided tan lasts longer than a normal tan
claims.believers: A seller-style post on T Nation says a melanotan tan can last two to three times as long as a normal tan [3].
claims.experts: Reference sources describe melanotan II stimulating melanogenesis but do not report durations compared with sun tans [1].

claims.claim: The peptide's size makes a nasal spray ineffective
claims.believers: A T Nation member said they kept reading that melanotan II's large molecular weight would leave a spray essentially useless [2].
claims.experts: No published study has examined nasal absorption of melanotan II for tanning.

card.summary: Needle-free melanotan sprays sold online; unlicensed, unregulated and untested by any published nasal-route study.
card.note: Unlicensed products; regulators in several countries warn against use and note possible impurities.

quick.overview:
Nasal tanning sprays are online products claiming to deliver melanotan peptides through the nose to darken skin without injections. They are not approved medicines.

No published studies were found on their effectiveness or content.
quick.mechanism: Melanotan-type peptides mimic alpha-MSH, a hormone that stimulates melanocytes to produce melanin. Whether sprays deliver meaningful amounts is undocumented in published research.
quick.risks: Regulators including the UK MHRA and US FDA have warned against unlicensed melanotan products. Reported effects of melanotan II include flushing, nausea and mole darkening, and product purity is unverified.

chain: Peptide analogue of alpha-MSH reaches the bloodstream
More melanin and a darker tan with less UV exposure
angle.text: Users want a deeper tan without long sun or sunbed sessions, and sellers promote nasal sprays as a needle-free route. Whether sprays deliver meaningful amounts is discussed in forums but not tested in published studies.
